extracted.intended_audience: general readers, journalists, advertisers, media students, media regulators
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and descriptive criteria for creating, recognizing, and assessing advertorials (advertisements presented in the form of editorial content) across print, web, TV, and radio. Covers types, appearance, tone, authorship, placement, legal disclosure, and ethical concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition — advertorial as advertisement disguised as editorial
rubrics_metrics.description: An advertorial is an advertisement in the form of editorial content. In printed publications, the advertisement is usually written to resemble an objective article and designed to ostensibly look like a legitimate and independent news story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Term is a blend of 'advertisement' and 'editorial' (portmanteau). Internet-based advertorials are linked to native advertising though synonymy is contested. Use this definition as the baseline for distinguishing advertorials from clear advertising or genuine editorial content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Type — Image advertorial
rubrics_metrics.description: Image advertorials: The organization running the advertisement wants to produce a favorable view of the organization or its products among the readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Purpose is brand- or reputation-building rather than conveying neutral information; expect promotional framing, favorable language, and examples/quotes that support a positive image.

rubrics_metrics.name: Type — Advocacy advertorial
rubrics_metrics.description: Advocacy advertorials: The organization wants to explain their view of a controversial subject.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These aim to influence public or policy debate; look for selective facts, framing to support an argument, and persuasive rhetorical devices rather than balanced reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Type — Journalism advertorial
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalism advertorials: The organization wants to attract media attention to a subject or themselves. Their goal may be inspiring independently written stories about their area of interest, to get quoted in related stories, or to influence how journalists will write about a subject in the future.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Often written to mimic news features to gain earned coverage; may include 'news hook' language and PR-style pitch elements. Evaluate intent to seed topics or sources for reporters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appearance and resemblance to editorial content
rubrics_metrics.description: Advertorials differ from traditional advertisements in that they are designed to resemble the editorial content of the publication in which they appear. Most publications prohibit advertisements that are identical in appearance to their regular articles. However, the distinctions between advertorials and editorial content may be subtle. Disclaimers such as the word 'advertisement' are sometimes included but are not always present.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check layout, fonts, paper stock (in print), placement, and explicit labels. Anti-patterns: advertorials that are visually indistinguishable from regular editorial content or that lack any clear label. Publishers may use alternative labels ('special promotional feature', 'special advertising section').

rubrics_metrics.name: Tone — promotional/press-release alignment
rubrics_metrics.description: The tone of an advertorial typically aligns more closely with that of a press release than with an objective journalistic article.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect promotional language, calls to action, product mentions, and one-sided reporting. Use tone as an indicator: neutral, investigative voice suggests editorial; enthusiastic, promotional voice suggests advertorial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorship and editorial control transparency
rubrics_metrics.description: Many newspapers and magazines will assign staff writers or freelancers to write advertorials, usually without a byline credit. A major difference between regular editorial and advertorial is that clients usually have content approval of advertorials, a luxury usually not provided with regular editorial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate byline presence, editorial independence, and whether the client had approval or provided content. Lack of byline combined with client approval is a transparency red flag.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integration with editorial to bypass blockers and enhance credibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Advertorials can be integrated with editorial content to bypass ad-blocking, enhance credibility and brand familiarity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Integration into editorial streams (native placement, sponsored sections) increases persuasive effect and risk of misleading audiences. Consider disclosure prominence and audience expectations when assessing legitimacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Television advertorial characteristics and conflict-avoidance
rubrics_metrics.description: Advertorials on television are longer than typical television advertisements. They are usually played on cable and satellite channels, may include a plot or story line to increase entertainment value, and are commonly used as segments on daytime programs featuring light talk. Advertorials are usually hosted by regular advertorial hosts who interact with business representatives; the main hosts usually do not interact with the advertorial hosts or business representatives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect longer format, narrative elements, product demonstrations, and placement on lower-cost cable/satellite slots. Best-practice: keep advertorial hosts separate from newsroom/newscast talent to avoid conflict of interest and audience confusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Radio advertorial characteristics
rubrics_metrics.description: On radio, advertorials can feature discussions between an announcer or a DJ and the representative of a business. The discussion may feature testimonials from customers or a personal endorsement from the announcer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Listen for conversational format, testimonials, endorsements, and host-read promotion. Historical scandals (e.g., 'cash for comment') illustrate the ethical risk when such material is presented as editorial commentary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal disclosure and labeling requirements (examples: UK ASA, US Postal Service/DMM)
rubrics_metrics.description: In the United Kingdom, the Advertising Standards Authority requires advertorials to be clearly marked as such. For magazines in the United States mailed at the publication rate, the Postal Service's Domestic Mail Manual states that under 18 USC 1734, if valuable consideration is paid for the publication of editorial matter that matter must be plainly marked 'advertisement' on the first page (with prominence and emphasis), with penalties for non-compliance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When producing or evaluating advertorials, follow jurisdictional disclosure rules: clearly label paid editorial, make the label prominent (on first page/promotion), and avoid misleading presentation. Use regulator guidance (ASA rulings, DMM 707/18 USC 1734) as compliance checklist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethical risks — potential to mislead and damage reputation
rubrics_metrics.description: Advertorials, especially those that are not clearly disclosed, are the subject of controversy in journalism ethics and marketing ethics. Researchers have found that they often mislead readers who are unaware of their origin; as many as two thirds of readers confuse advertorials for reporting (2016 study).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess audience confusion risk, institutional reputation harm, and the need for critical literacy. Publishers should ensure disclosure and separation; readers should be educated to identify paid content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relation to native advertising and classification issues
rubrics_metrics.description: The concept of internet-based advertorials is linked to native advertising; however, whether the two terms are synonymous is contested.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When categorizing or regulating online sponsored content, examine format, labeling, and intent rather than relying on label alone. The contested boundary affects how content should be disclosed and governed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intent — goals of advertorial placement
rubrics_metrics.description: Advertorials may be placed to inspire independently written stories, to get quoted in related stories, or to influence how journalists will write about a subject in the future.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate advertorials for strategic PR intent (seeding topics/sources) vs. simple product promotion; this informs both ethical assessment and how prominently disclosure should be made.
